newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT - Aussie on the ropes, fearing rate blow.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Aussie on the ropes, fearing rate blow.

text.p: *AUD pinned near 75 cents after choppy night saw good offers soaked up at first by corporate bids but unable to clear $0.7530
*NY banks, IMM names sold it back but rumour of offshore bid for an Australian financial institution offered support
*Market on alert for another RBA easing, perhaps as soon as this morning, in wake of Thursday's dire jobs data
By 8.00 am (2200 GMT) the dollar had huddled at US$0.7507/12 having slid to US$0.7515/20 late Thursday from US$0.7590/95 the day before.

It did try and bounce overnight on coporate bids and buying from a name thought to be protecting a big binary option with a strike at 75 cents, but only made US$0.7530 before New York and IMM options players sold again.

Some support was provided by rumours an offshore bank was about to bid for an Australian financial institution -- the main name in the frame being ING and the target either ANZ or AMP -- which if true would imply a need to buy dollars as well.
Such a prospect would matter little, however, should the RBA ease today and take official rates here below those of the U.S. for the first time since the dollar was floated in 1983.
Market rates to three years have already made the transition with the September 90-day bank bill future at 94.91, a 25 basis point rise in two days, implying a rate of 5.09 percent.

Dealers also suspected an immediate easing would only leave the market hungry for more and bill rates would move to price in yet another, that would be the sixth in the cycle no less. Such a yawning gap in A$/US$ interest differentials could well suck the local currency down to US$0.7380 or even 73 cents.

There was also a risk U.S. rates would be heading higher, although a surprisingly soft retail sales report for May released overnight made it a little less likely the Federal Reserve would hike at its next meeting on July 1-2.
Even that news was double-edged for the A$ since the less the chance of a U.S. tightening the more confident the RBA may be it could cut without sending the currency into free-fall.

As if all this were not bearish enough, dealers reported increasing unease about the risk of a drought in Australia due to the El Nino weather pattern, which could be expected to hurt agricultural exports. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
